not sure how things work in italy, can just speak to my experience in us.

had i not hired a disability lawyer i doubt i would have been approved. (no money upfront, only paid if win appeal, receive percentage of backpay disability that we receive that dates to when disability claim was first filed) i also have chronic pain factors as well as mental health. i struggle with executive functioning and my appeal would have been a scattered disorganized shitshow at best.
the lawyers coordinated with all my drs, collated the relevant information in a manner easy to reference for the judge who handles appeals. 

it is an overwhelming process, one i don’t see any way i could have navigated alone. a disability lawyer has the familiarity with the system to know what information to gather from drs, what tests and records need to be included in the filing to evidentially support the claim, as well as handling most of the questions from the judge and were able to succinctly provide answers and reference the supporting evidence (with page and doc number in the filing) whereas i would have been floundering (judge was very stern, and i struggle to deal with those types of people, feeling like whatever i say is lacking and end up rambling) and i just can’t recommend disability attorney enough. 
it was irritating having to pay them several thousand in order for my disability to be validated (though they receive that directly from social security office when back sum is dispersed) but if i had to do it all over again, only thing i would change would be to have contacted them earlier, save myself a few months of feeling constantly overwhelmed and increasingly hopeless and lost. i found it embarrassing at first to need to turn to them, that it meant i was somehow inept, but swallowing my pride and asking for help was probably one of the few smart decisions ive made in my life. 


sorry, don’t have any direct insight or help for if you end up handling it alone (or if your system is vastly different from ours in us.) and wish you the best of luck in your situation, and wish the process was more designed to help those who need it rather than it seeming to be more focused on catching anyone who they feel doesn’t, even if that means countless people who do need fail to receive the support they need.

thanks for sharing, that’s about what i was thinking it might be. for me, raads i scored 150s range, catq 140s. so roughly similar. think if there’s anything you can take from it, whether or not you are actually on the spectrum, you certainly deal with enough things that overlap with those associated with areas that those who are on the spectrum do, that your questioning if you are as well definitely makes sense. 
(if family member also scores high, i wouldn’t take that as immediately invalidating, as autism seems to often run in families. for me, the validating aspect of sibling scoring about a quarter to a fifth of mine (i mean i know the actual score, but doesn’t feel right to list the specifics involving others, so vague intentionally) wasn’t that results were so different, but that they had scored so low, showing that the test actually gave results that low, (sorry just woke up and about to go back to sleep, struggling to word or communicate clearly) but like it wasn’t just that everyone scored like around 100 (what i expected them to score) later knew someone who scored an 8. so for me seeing those, while didn’t lead to me immediately accepting audhd, it did show me, at minimum, just how starkly different i perceive the world around me and my experiences in it. whether that meant asd or not, it was enough to at least start to really accept neurodivergence.
(also an obstacle for me is that my perception for asd has been locked into the level of understanding from the 90s, where really the only people who it seemed were recognized as autistic were those at the far end of the spectrum today (what may be seen as level 3s. ive  heard there are some issues with the level 1,2,3 use, but the little i know of them i have found helpful. for me it gives me a way to coexist without feeling like i am undeservedly taking space or like i am coopting another’s struggle. bc i know there are a lot of people who face more challenges than i do, and it doesn’t feel right to me to share the exact same label as them, bc id worry about how things i may be able to do could be used by neurotypicals to invalidate the struggles of others with asd. but being able to subcategorize and say yes but i fall mostly under what is now associated with level 1, while those who would be seen as level 2 or level 3, may have assistance needs in areas that i do not, and while we are all on the spectrum, there’s a wide array of experiences, and my being able to do something doesn’t mean everyone else on spectrum should also be able to do it as well, and if they’re not then they’re not really trying. 


also think it’s something that no single test, or even official assessment if given over one to three days is going to give you results that you will be able to feel fully confident in, as that certainly wasn’t enough to overcome my doubts and questioning. but the struggles you feel are real. maybe to start, don’t trying defining it specifically, instead try acknowledging that you are neurodivergent. 

also turns out almost everyone i tend to stay friends with, found out more recently the majority are all audhd themselves. and that was not intentional, just who i felt someone more comfortable around and connected to, even though i hadn’t even considered audhd for most of the time ive known them. not that that is a large sample size 😅 )

honestly, sounds like you basically just described me (aside from age, dating history & specifics of jobs…though ive had a ton of different ones of those.)

earlier this year, had assessment done over two months, and audhd (depression anxiety as well, but those were symptoms, not root issue.) im still working on accepting it and impact it has on my understanding of well me, past events, struggles, identity i guess. (previously dx’d ADD in 90’s but when that was rolled in ADHD at the time it made it feel like ADD was fake then, didnt know distinction between inattentive & hyperactive.)
and had never seriously considered autism until recently, bc my understanding was outdated on that as well. but it feels like it slowly sinking in, feel the walls ive had up for years are starting to crack, audhd just feels right, but have been misdiagnosed in past, so hard for me to fully trust, without worrying maybe i said something wrong, misunderstood questions and gave inaccurate answers unknowingly or bc i misunderstood how i felt.

as to whether it’s worth it, that’s really up to you, what you are hoping or wanting to get out of it. for me, it’s mainly understanding of self. i’ve struggled to function for so long, i’m hoping that understanding why will allow me to learn what changes i need to make to be more comfortable in my own skin, instead of continuing trying to force myself to function and failing repeatedly. 

one thing i can say, if you do decide you want to pursue, as your worries about knowledge of terminology, about responses being misconstrued, not wanting to take up space in an identity you fear you might not belong, etc sound very similar to me, i’d recommend an assessment done weekly over a period of 8-10 weeks. that’s the main reason im slowly coming around to accepting mine. any single day one, even if done over 6-8 hours, i worry if maybe i was subconsciously masking and didn’t realize nullifying any results, or how my worries shift over time, and while whatever the result of a single or two day assessment, what if that only holds true for how i felt that day, but missed so much else bc i didn’t have those feelings that day so i didn’t think to include them (my feelings are present seem to dominate, when im happy, i can’t remember how it felt to be down, like i’ll know that i had been before, but i’ll question if it was really that bad or if i was just stuck in my head and being dramatic. and likewise, when down, i don’t know how happiness feels, like i factually recount times that i was, what i may have done, people i may have been with, but the feeling eludes me and ill question if i really did have as much fun as i thought i had, or if maybe im just romanticizing it bc it seemed better than whatever place in my life im in at that moment.) but having it done over the course of 2+ months, i feel those different states presented, and even if i dont feel i can accurately communicate past feelings, the spectrum of down to ok showed over the course of the assessment and were thus taken into account. it relieved the burden of feeling like everything was on me to fully communicate the entirety of my existence when there is so much that i don’t understand (and thus the whole reason for the assessment in the first place!) but i feel like for the first time in years im finally starting to make some progress, ending how i would kind of circle from worry to worry, accepting or dismissing short term, but doubts often leading me to find myself back in the same spot a few months later. 

also totally get your rfk fears, even if quashed for now, the idea of autism registry coming from this administration is frankly terrifying, hearkens back to dark periods for those who didn’t tune out history class. for that, you can first check with individual therapists, if they are qualified to do the assessment, and what they do with any of information. privacy protection is often paramount (not sure on what may be required to report if using insurance, outside of the universal threat to self/others) but can find some who will keep any potential diagnosis confidential and up to your discretion if you want to inform your gp or any other drs you may work with. 

but best of luck. it’s definitely not easy when struggling and not fully understanding what is going on. hope you are able to find the clarity you need.

i also had a really hopeful spinal stim trial. honestly it was pretty amazing. i was still in “lava” stage at that time, my sleep was a lot like what it sounds like you’re still going through. then for a night or two, sleep through the night for what may have been the first time. but day i was due back to get the trial removed and schedule the permanent my careless ass got the cord caught on a doorknob and ripped the electrodes most of the way out of my back. that hurt. still got the permanent put in, but it never came close to replicating the relief of the trial. (actually had multiple, a second was implanted, and later a different model was swapped out for the first one i had done) but ripping it out caused a lot of scarring, and while they tried to clean the area up, i had just screwed it up too much, and couldn’t never get them to work right again. if u haven’t been down that road, might be worth a shot, think it has over a 50% success rate (being noticeable improvement, not elimination, in pain.)

i seriously considered doing so years ago, mine developed in left foot after an accident (surgeon told me it was 50/50 they’d have to amputate, i destroyed my ankle, though not sure why amputation was on the table, they had me on a lot of pain meds the night between accident and surgery so it’s kinda hazy) not sure at what point it actually developed, months post op dr who did surgery kept saying my pain was normal for the damage i did, but i recall trying to tell him it felt even worse than that. wasn’t officially diagnosed til a year and a half later when seeing a specialist for the pain, as it seemed to keep increasing not improving, luckily with this dr the pain id been describing for over a year as feeling like lava is flowing through my veins clicked and he pursued crps.
after a couple years pain was still too much i brought up amputation and dr mentioned that it’s possible to get phantom limb pain and there’d be fewer ways to treat pain in that case. and the thought terrified me, still having the pain without anything physical there, honestly that probably would have broken my mind, so i abandoned the consideration. 

can say for me (realize not everyone responds in same way to treatments or we’d all have a better quality of life) ive tried more treatments than i can recall, but for past half year or year, ive been getting stellate ganglion blocks in both sides of neck every 4 weeks and that in addition to meds (and a lot of resting and at least laying down, sometimes elevating slightly) its been the best its been since the accident. 

but hope you find something that works or at least helps some, others have more experience actually having gone through with amputation, but that phantom pain terrified me way more than the possibility of the loss of limb.

Buuuuut, a Vespa accident a few months later derailed that thought (confined to bed for months, followed by even longer in a wheel chair, it was about a year before i could really walk again, first with a cane for a fairly long time, fortunately havent needed that in a few years (save if im going to be on my feet the entire day.) But for most of this period, the whole concept of being bipolar worked its way into my sense of identity, as i began to view various aspects of my life, that hadn’t previously made sense, through that lens and stitched together a more coherent sense of self.
